conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way.  

Today I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand your experience so we can support you best.  

Everything you share stays between you and the care team unless you tell us something that makes us worry about immediate safety, and then we’ll talk together about the next steps. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to begin?

**Question 1:**  
In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

It’s…different now. I can still smile at, say, a cute photo or when the baby grips my finger, but the spark is pretty muted. Most things that used to feel fun—like chatting with friends or even watching a show—just seem flat. I’ll do them hoping they’ll lift me up, but the enjoyment is only a fraction of what it was before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself letting out a little laugh—like when my husband makes a joke or when the baby makes a funny face—but it feels kind of forced, like I’m going through the motions. The humor doesn’t really land the way it used to, and the smile fades fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but mostly I just feel kind of numb or worried ahead of time. It’s like I’m hoping I’ll enjoy it, but the actual looking-forward feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I ate, or that I’m not soothing her right. Even spilling a little pumped milk had me in tears because it felt like proof I’m failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be doing. I know, rationally, babies cry and accidents happen, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. My mind keeps spinning “what-ifs” about the baby—like whether she’s breathing okay in the bassinet or if that sniffle is something worse—even when everything looks fine. There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits there and won’t turn off, especially at night.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week it’s felt like a wave rushing over me—my heart races, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment it feels like I’m trapped in my own body with no clear reason why.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… it feels like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, texts go unanswered, and even basic stuff like showering feels like climbing a mountain. I’ll look at the day ahead and think, “How am I supposed to get through all this?”—and then I feel guilty for feeling that way, because I only have one little baby, not five.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s hard to fall asleep most nights. Even when the baby’s settled, my mind keeps circling—worrying I missed something, replaying every little noise she made. Once I do drift off, I wake up with a jolt of anxiety at least once or twice, and then it takes forever to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty often, yeah. It’s like a heaviness that just sits on me. I’ll look at her sleeping and still feel this ache or emptiness, and some mornings I wake up already teary. It isn’t every single moment, but it’s definitely there most of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened maybe once or twice this week. Little things set me off—like running out of diapers and having to drag us to the store, or when I couldn’t get her to latch right. I’ll just feel this rush of sadness and the tears come before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has popped into my head a couple of times, mostly when everything feels like too much. Like, I’ll be standing at the sink and suddenly picture just not being here anymore—but I haven’t made any plan or anything. I push it away because I know I don’t really want to leave her; it just scares me that the thought shows up at all.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has dimmed since your baby arrived: smiles feel forced, excitement is replaced by worry, and even basic tasks can feel overwhelming. Nights are long with racing thoughts, sudden waves of panic catch you off guard, and a heavy sadness lingers most days. You described blaming yourself for every hiccup, crying over small setbacks, and being frightened by passing thoughts of not wanting to be here-thoughts you stressed you don't want to act on, yet they frighten you all the same.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can only manage brief, forced laughter and reports the enjoyment is markedly diminished and fleeting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-absence of anticipatory enjoyment (“numb or worried ahead of time”) matching “Hardly at all”</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring frequently and intensely across multiple situations, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily persistent, intrusive worry without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Clear description of sudden, intense panic attacks with racing heart and breathlessness happening multiple times this week.</sym>, <sym>"Barely treading water," inability to complete basic tasks, and feeling overwhelmed match "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep disruption with racing thoughts and repeated anxious awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent sadness and emotional pain most of the day, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive suicidal thoughts occurring multiple times, matching 'Sometimes</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the EPDS threshold (≥14) indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with prominent <sym>anxiety</sym>. You endorse core symptoms: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, and recurrent thoughts of death (DSM-5 Criterion A). These symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment in functioning and have persisted beyond two weeks (Criterion B). The presence of <sym>panic attacks</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> heightens risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Request comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and safety planning
3. Inform a trusted adult nearby about these thoughts for support until professional help is in place
4. Avoid being alone with the baby when overwhelmed-set up a buddy system
5. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
6. Begin gentle daily routine: 5-minute outdoor walk, balanced meals, and accept help with housework or night feeds
7. Practice 4-7-8 breathing at night; turn phone off 30 min before bed to aid sleep
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor response to treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire, self-report, 2–3 wks postpartum

Symptoms/observations endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2) – humor feels forced, anticipatory enjoyment absent  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3) – attributes infant fussing or minor mishaps to personal failure  
- Persistent, uncontrolled worry and nocturnal ruminations (Q4, Q7)  
- Discrete panic-like episodes (Q5) – sudden surges of fear, racing heart, breathlessness, no clear precipitant  
- Overwhelm and functional impairment (Q6) – basic self-care feels insurmountable  
- Daily low mood with frequent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance disturbance linked to mood (Q7)  
- Passive self-harm ideation without plan (Q10) – transient images of “not being here” when distressed; patient denies intent but acknowledges distress about the thoughts themselves

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with infant care and self-care, and have persisted ≥2 wks. No current psychotic features or manic symptoms reported.

Risk flags:
- Depressed mood + anhedonia + guilt  
- Anxiety with panic attacks  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Passive suicidal thoughts (safety concern)

Screening impression: High likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; active safety risk due to presence of self-harm thoughts. Recommend immediate comprehensive assessment (EPDS score calculation, clinical interview, collateral history) and safety planning.
